name: Affine logic
intro: Much like the linear logic, affine logic allows for a restricted subset of operations,
namely, it can swap, discard, and compose terms, but not duplicate them.
It is therefore not Turing complete, which may actually be beneficial in some applications.

content.name: Identity
intro: Unlike in linear logic, identity is not required to be present in the initial set.
This is because discarding is allowed and either K x <something> or
some variant of KI can be built.
Create identity from B, K and T combinators.
(C would've been too easy...)

content.name: To rule them all
intro: Create a monobasis for affine logic.
I made mine by taking x→x, attaching random affine combinators to the right,
plugging the resulting function into itself, and shaking it violently.

input.name: X
input.note: Declare your own combinator X. It should not duplicate variables.

content.name: Triple trouble
intro: Think making W from M was hard?
This time you need to construct a non-duplicating term φ that,
given triple = x->x x x, produces M = x->x x:
φ triple x = x x

content.name: Head and shoulders
intro: Given a function f, build a new function g such that
g (V x (V y ( ... ))) = f x y, and the tail is discarded.
Easy if you can duplicate the list! But it's forbidden.

content.name: Limited supply
intro: It's trivial to duplicate two variables if you can use duplicating terms,
such as W or M, multiple times.
But what if you can only use such term once?
Build a non-duplicating function φ
such that φ W a b = a a (b b).

content.name: Taming the infinity
intro: You are given a non-terminating fixed-point combinator, Y:
Y f = f(Y f) = f(f(Y f)) = ....
Build an affine combinator f that converts Y to M:
f Y x = x x.

content.name: Affine numbers design
intro: Although Church numerals are powerful, they aren't the only way to represent numbers
in combinatory logic. Multiple systems with different properties exist,
each with its own advantages and drawbacks.
This time we'd like to emphasise the following features:
• the numbers themselves should be affine (no argument duplication),
• decrement should be O(1),
• and number <n> should extract the <n>-th element of a list,
if it exists: (cons a (cons b ...(cons z nil)...)) <n> = list[n] (assuming zero-based indexing).
Define zero and succ such that <n> succ zero
represents the number <n>, as well as pred and iszero,
all of which should be affine.
Additionally, a non-affine fold function should be provided:
fold <n> f x = (f (f ...{n times}... (f x) ...)).
Although such a function cannot have a normal form in the strict sense,
at least fold, fold <n>, and fold <n> f
should terminate under call-by-name reduction strategy.
Spoiler alert: you are most likely to end up with a variant of the
Scott numerals.
